paras: The clubbing of Tom Wilson was a police beating in Wadesboro, North Carolina, in about early August 1881, when two town policemen knocked Wilson, a Black man, senseless with their clubs while arresting him. A crowd of Black residents then rushed the officers, and the sheriff, the town marshal and a judge intervened; the only surviving report presented the affair as an "ugly sequel" to a political speech.
The incident followed a speech by Oliver Dockery at Wadesboro and was printed in a column of "Election Echoes" that also discussed how the Black vote had helped defeat prohibition.

Policemen Bruner and Brower arrested Wilson for "an indecency on the street, and violation of town laws." According to the Times, he resisted and "snapped a pistol once or twice at the officers," and they knocked him senseless with their clubs. The account comes only from the officers' side; no version from Wilson or from witnesses appears in the coverage.

A crowd of Black residents, described as "a mob of negroes" crying "for blood and murder," then rushed the policemen, who fled into their homes. Sheriff T. J. Hardison faced the crowd until Marshal Tomlinson arrived with an armed posse, and Judge R. Tyler Bennett rode up on horseback and commanded the peace. At Bennett's direction the two policemen were taken to the courthouse and lodged in jail overnight so that the crowd could disperse.
Wilson was reported "not badly hurt" and walked home several miles into the country after the affray. No report of charges against Wilson, the officers or members of the crowd was found.

The story survives in one white weekly, the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic of August 11, 1881, which credited it to the Times. The paper took the officers' account as fact, praised the sheriff for having "bravely faced the mob," and spoke of "drunken negroes" who needed to "cool off." Its concern was the crowd rather than the beating: it urged that the "ringleaders" be arrested and set to breaking rock, or else Wadesboro should "repeal all law, and dismiss her police."
